_metadata.purpose: x02 single revision round: every reviewed x02 hint; reviewerFlaggedProblem marks the concrete problems the independent reviewers raised

items.reviewerReason: Both the Magic Carpet and the Genie are Aladdin's companions in the story and the Disney film; instant on both sides.
items.pairNote: Easy but clean; the obvious hint is the right one here.

current.wordAConnection: Aladdin rides the Magic Carpet
current.wordBConnection: Aladdin frees the Genie from the lamp
current.revealExplanation: Carpet and Genie are both Aladdin's loyal sidekicks.

items.reviewerReason: Mario is famously a plumber, and pipes are a plumber's stock in trade (plus Mario's warp pipes), so both sides click.
items.pairNote: Solid, fair, mildly playful.

current.wordAConnection: Mario is a plumber by trade
current.wordBConnection: Plumbers work with pipes
current.revealExplanation: Mario is a plumber, which explains all those green pipes.

items.reviewerReason: A bishop is a chess piece and a church official; a true double meaning that lands at once.
items.pairNote: Model hint of the style the owner wants.

current.wordAConnection: A bishop is a chess piece that moves diagonally
current.wordBConnection: A bishop is a senior church leader
current.revealExplanation: The bishop has a job on the chessboard and in the church.

items.reviewerReason: Jack and the Beanstalk: Jack climbs the beanstalk and meets the giant at the top.
items.pairNote: Clean story link.

current.wordAConnection: A giant lives at the top of the beanstalk
current.wordBConnection: Jack climbs the beanstalk
current.revealExplanation: Jack climbed the beanstalk and ran into a very grumpy giant.

items.reviewerReason: Oscar the Grouch lives in a trash can and the Oscar is Hollywood's trophy; two unrelated Oscars meet neatly.
items.pairNote: One of the strongest in the batch.

current.wordAConnection: Oscar the Grouch lives in a trash can
current.wordBConnection: An Oscar is Hollywood's most famous trophy
current.revealExplanation: One Oscar lives in a trash can; the other sits on a mantel.

items.reviewerReason: Billy goat and Billy the Kid are both instantly familiar, and the extra layer (a kid is a baby goat) makes this phrase-join satisfying rather than mechanical.
items.pairNote: A phrase-join, but one of the exceptional kind the owner still accepts.

current.wordAConnection: A male goat is a billy goat
current.wordBConnection: Billy the Kid was a famous outlaw
current.revealExplanation: Billy the Kid meets the billy goat, and a kid is a baby goat too.

items.reviewerReason: The classic joke 'Why did the chicken cross the road?' supplies both words in one breath.
items.pairNote: Very easy, but fair and a little fun.

current.wordAConnection: Why did the chicken cross the road?
current.wordBConnection: The chicken got to the other side of the road
current.revealExplanation: Why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the other side.

items.reviewerReason: King Kong battled Godzilla on film (1962 and 2021) and famously climbed the Empire State Building.
items.pairNote: Strong pop-culture link.

current.wordAConnection: Godzilla battled Kong on the big screen
current.wordBConnection: King Kong climbed the Empire State Building
current.revealExplanation: Kong fought Godzilla and famously scaled a skyscraper.

items.reviewerReason: Squidward is SpongeBob's neighbor, and despite his name he is officially an octopus; the octopus side is a surprise fact that delivers a great reveal.
items.pairNote: Works best if no SQUID tile is on the board to mislead.

current.wordAConnection: Despite his name, Squidward is an octopus
current.wordBConnection: Squidward is SpongeBob's grumpy neighbor
current.revealExplanation: Surprise: SpongeBob's neighbor Squidward is an octopus, not a squid.

items.reviewerReason: Rapunzel is locked in a tower and lets down her long hair; both are the heart of the tale.
items.pairNote: Clean and fair.

current.wordAConnection: Rapunzel has impossibly long hair
current.wordBConnection: Rapunzel is locked away in a tower
current.revealExplanation: Rapunzel let down her hair from the tower window.

items.reviewerReason: The Statue of Liberty (dedicated 1886) is the statue, and her raised torch is its defining feature.
items.pairNote: Straightforward; the explanation's date is correct.

current.wordAConnection: The Statue of Liberty stands in New York Harbor
current.wordBConnection: Lady Liberty holds a torch high
current.revealExplanation: The Statue of Liberty has held her torch high since 1886.

items.reviewerReason: Morning dew and Mountain Dew are both instantly familiar, and the nature-versus-soda twist gives this phrase-join a real click.
items.reviewerFix: Replace 'fills cans of Mountain Dew' with 'gives Mountain Dew its name' so the explanation does not read as a literal claim about what is in the can.
items.pairNote: Phrase-join passed as exceptional; a second opinion could reasonably call it BORDERLINE under the fewer-phrase-joins guidance.

current.wordAConnection: Morning dew covers the grass at sunrise
current.wordBConnection: Mountain Dew is a popular soda
current.revealExplanation: Dew forms on morning grass and fills cans of Mountain Dew.

items.reviewerReason: The Esc (Escape) key sits on every keyboard, and escape is what prisoners plot; a neat double meaning.
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: Every keyboard has an Escape key
current.wordBConnection: Prisoners dream of an escape
current.revealExplanation: Esc on your keyboard, escape from prison.

items.reviewerReason: A runway is both the catwalk for fashion shows and the strip planes take off from.
items.pairNote: One of the batch's best double meanings.

current.wordAConnection: Models strut down the fashion runway
current.wordBConnection: Planes take off from a runway
current.revealExplanation: One runway is for supermodels; the other is for jumbo jets.

items.reviewerReason: Dumbo is the circus elephant whose huge ears let him fly; both targets are central to the film.
items.pairNote: Clean.

current.wordAConnection: Dumbo is the circus's baby elephant
current.wordBConnection: Dumbo flies using his enormous ears
current.revealExplanation: Dumbo went from circus outcast to star by flying with his huge ears.

items.reviewerReason: Jumanji is a magical board game (later a video game) that unleashes the jungle on its players.
items.pairNote: Solid.

current.wordAConnection: Jumanji is a magical board game
current.wordBConnection: Jumanji unleashes the jungle, and one sequel is Welcome to the Jungle
current.revealExplanation: Roll the dice in Jumanji and the jungle comes to you.

items.reviewerReason: Smurfs are famously blue and live in mushroom houses; the mushroom side is a pleasing detail.
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: Smurfs are little blue people
current.wordBConnection: Smurfs live in mushroom houses
current.revealExplanation: The Smurfs are blue and live in houses shaped like mushrooms.

items.reviewerReason: Dory's short-term memory loss and her 'just keep swimming' motto cover both targets.
items.pairNote: Excellent.

current.wordAConnection: Dory has short-term memory loss
current.wordBConnection: Dory's motto is "Just keep swimming"
current.revealExplanation: Dory forgets everything except to just keep swimming.

items.reviewerReason: Hercules is the byword for strength, and as Zeus's son he earns a place on Mount Olympus (the goal of the Disney film); the hint works but the explanation never mentions Olympus.
items.reviewerFix: Rewrite as 'Zeus's son Hercules used his legendary strength to earn his place on Mount Olympus.' so both targets are explained.
items.pairNote: Good hint with a one-sided explanation; fix the text.

current.wordAConnection: Hercules is a son of Zeus, who rules from Mount Olympus
current.wordBConnection: Hercules is famous for his strength
current.revealExplanation: Hercules went from zero to hero with legendary strength.

items.reviewerReason: Horseshoes and leprechauns are both luck symbols, and Lucky Charms (Lucky the Leprechaun, horseshoe marshmallows) doubles the link.
items.pairNote: Two routes reinforce each other; strong.

current.wordAConnection: A horseshoe is a lucky charm
current.wordBConnection: Lucky the Leprechaun is the Lucky Charms mascot
current.revealExplanation: Lucky Charms has a leprechaun mascot and horseshoe marshmallows.

items.reviewerReason: TONY completes Tony Hawk, the world's most famous skateboarder, covering both sides; but the claim he 'made skateboarding famous' overstates history.
items.reviewerFix: Rewrite as 'Tony Hawk, skateboarding's biggest star, landed the first 900 in 1999.' to avoid the overstatement.
items.pairNote: Leans on a first-name fill-in for HAWK, but the skateboard side makes it a person-reference rather than a mechanical join.

current.wordAConnection: Tony Hawk is the surname that matches
current.wordBConnection: Tony Hawk is a skateboarding legend
current.revealExplanation: Tony Hawk made skateboarding famous with the first 900 trick.

items.reviewerReason: Bigfoot is a legendary monster and also the name of the original, most famous monster truck.
items.pairNote: Great find; the truck side may surprise some players, which adds to the payoff.

current.wordAConnection: Bigfoot is a legendary forest monster
current.wordBConnection: Bigfoot was the first monster truck
current.revealExplanation: Bigfoot is both a mythical monster and the original monster truck.

items.reviewerReason: Mount Rushmore names the mount, and Washington's is the leftmost (and first completed) of its four faces.
items.pairNote: Fair; 'first of four' is accurate reading left to right.

current.wordAConnection: Mount Rushmore is a carved mountain in South Dakota
current.wordBConnection: George Washington's face is carved on Mount Rushmore
current.revealExplanation: Washington's face is the first of four on Mount Rushmore.

items.reviewerReason: The tongue twister links both, but PETER alone pulls toward Peter Pan, Peter Parker or Peter Rabbit before Peter Piper, so it points less sharply than PIPER.
items.pairNote: Serve PIPER; PETER is the weaker variant of the same idea.

current.wordAConnection: Peter Piper picked peppers
current.wordBConnection: Peter Piper's peppers were pickled
current.revealExplanation: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.

items.reviewerReason: PIPER summons 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers' almost uniquely, and its P-sounds echo both targets.
items.pairNote: Serve PIPER; PETER is the weaker variant of the same idea.

current.wordAConnection: Peter Piper picked a peck of peppers
current.wordBConnection: The peppers in the tongue twister were pickled
current.revealExplanation: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers. Try saying it fast.

items.reviewerReason: Perry the Platypus from Phineas and Ferb is secretly the spy Agent P.
items.pairNote: Strongest for players under about 30; older players may need the explanation.

current.wordAConnection: Perry is the platypus in Phineas and Ferb
current.wordBConnection: Perry is secretly Agent P, a spy
current.revealExplanation: Perry the Platypus leads a secret life as Agent P.

items.reviewerReason: Sub and hero are both names for the long sandwich; the sub side is instant and the hero side is the small reveal.
items.pairNote: Plain but fair; the 'hero is a sandwich too' realisation gives it a modest click.

current.wordAConnection: A hero is a long sandwich
current.wordBConnection: A sub is a long sandwich
current.revealExplanation: Hero or sub, it is the same long sandwich with a different name.

items.reviewerReason: You use a browser to get on the internet, and Safari is Apple's browser; the explanation only covers the Safari side and misses the nicer Internet Explorer angle.
items.reviewerFix: Rewrite as 'Internet Explorer and Safari are both web browsers.' so both targets are explained.
items.pairNote: Mirror of the owner's INTERNET + AFRICA -> SAFARI example; fine.

current.wordAConnection: You browse the internet
current.wordBConnection: Safari is Apple's web browser
current.revealExplanation: Safari is a browser, not just an African adventure.

items.reviewerReason: Ireland is the Emerald Isle and the Wizard of Oz rules the Emerald City; two famous green nicknames meet.
items.pairNote: Strong; the wizard side takes one step (Oz) but it is a very familiar step.

current.wordAConnection: Ireland is called the Emerald Isle
current.wordBConnection: The Wizard of Oz lives in the Emerald City
current.revealExplanation: The Emerald Isle and the Emerald City are both very green.

items.reviewerReason: The Powerpuff Girls were made from sugar, spice and everything nice (plus Chemical X), per the show's famous intro.
items.pairNote: Fun, accurate pop-culture link.

current.wordAConnection: The Powerpuff Girls were made with spice
current.wordBConnection: The Powerpuff Girls were made with sugar
current.revealExplanation: Sugar, spice, everything nice, and Chemical X made the Powerpuff Girls.

items.reviewerReason: Acorns are the oak's seed and the squirrel's favourite stash; the idea is sound, but 'every mighty oak' starting from a squirrel's forgotten acorn overstates the fact.
items.reviewerFix: Rewrite as 'Oaks grow from acorns, and squirrels bury acorns, then forget a few that sprout into new oaks.' to keep the charm without the false 'every'.
items.pairNote: Good hint; tidy the hyperbole in the explanation.

current.wordAConnection: Acorns grow on oak trees
current.wordBConnection: Squirrels bury acorns for winter
current.revealExplanation: Every mighty oak starts as an acorn a squirrel forgot to dig up.

items.reviewerReason: Hens peck at feed, and a peck is a quick kiss; a sweet, exact double meaning.
items.pairNote: Excellent, low-key style.

current.wordAConnection: Hens peck at their food
current.wordBConnection: A peck is a quick kiss
current.revealExplanation: A hen pecks for seeds; a peck on the cheek is a little kiss.

items.reviewerReason: Clowns perform slapstick and a pie in the face is the genre's signature gag; the scene ties both.
items.pairNote: Fair; slightly broader than the others, but the pie-in-the-face image makes it click.

current.wordAConnection: Clowns are masters of slapstick
current.wordBConnection: A pie in the face is classic slapstick
current.revealExplanation: Nothing says slapstick like a clown taking a pie to the face.

items.reviewerReason: Belle falls for the Beast, and his gift of the castle library is one of the film's best-loved scenes.
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: Belle falls for the Beast
current.wordBConnection: The Beast gives book-loving Belle his huge library
current.revealExplanation: Belle fell for the Beast, and his library sure helped.

items.reviewerReason: Bill Nye the Science Guy names both targets, and the theme-song chant in the explanation is a nice touch.
items.pairNote: Strong for a U.S. audience.

current.wordAConnection: Bill Nye is the first name match
current.wordBConnection: Bill Nye the Science Guy
current.revealExplanation: Bill! Bill! Bill! Bill Nye the Science Guy.

items.reviewerReason: A tea kettle whistles when the water boils; one kitchen scene covers both.
items.pairNote: Plain but satisfying.

current.wordAConnection: You boil water for tea in a kettle
current.wordBConnection: A kettle whistles when the water boils
current.revealExplanation: The kettle whistles to tell you the tea water is ready.

items.reviewerReason: Gulliver is a giant among the tiny Lilliputians (and tiny among Brobdingnag's giants), so both sizes are his story.
items.pairNote: Explanation is accurate; mentioning Brobdingnag too would make it even nicer but is optional.

current.wordAConnection: Gulliver is a giant to the people of Lilliput
current.wordBConnection: The Lilliputians are tiny
current.revealExplanation: In Lilliput, ordinary Gulliver was a giant among tiny people.

items.reviewerReason: Willy Wonka is the candy maker, and the golden tickets hidden in his bars drive the story.
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: Willy Wonka makes candy in his factory
current.wordBConnection: Golden tickets were hidden in Wonka bars
current.revealExplanation: Find a golden ticket in a Wonka bar and the factory doors open.

items.reviewerReason: The hint itself is good (Cinderella must flee the ball at midnight, and the Times Square ball lands at midnight), but the explanation says midnight 'starts' the ball drop, when the drop begins at 11:59 and ends at midnight.
items.reviewerFix: Rewrite as 'Midnight ends Cinderella's night at the ball, and it's when the New Year's ball finishes its drop.' to correct the fact.
items.pairNote: Failed only for the false explanation; the hint idea is fine and the fix is a one-line rewrite.

current.wordAConnection: The New Year's Eve ball drops at midnight
current.wordBConnection: Cinderella must leave the ball by midnight
current.revealExplanation: Midnight ends Cinderella's ball and starts the New Year's ball drop.

items.reviewerReason: Mowgli is the jungle boy of The Jungle Book, which Kipling set in the jungles of India; the jungle side is instant and the India side clicks once explained.
items.pairNote: India side is the weaker half but true and fair.

current.wordAConnection: The Jungle Book is set in India
current.wordBConnection: Mowgli is raised in the jungle by wolves
current.revealExplanation: Mowgli, the boy from The Jungle Book, grew up in the jungles of India.

items.reviewerReason: The Little Mermaid's Ariel lives under the sea and gives up her voice to be with Prince Eric.
items.pairNote: Clean.

current.wordAConnection: Ariel falls for Prince Eric
current.wordBConnection: Ariel is a mermaid who lives under the sea
current.revealExplanation: Ariel traded her voice to leave the sea for Prince Eric.

items.reviewerReason: Ronald McDonald is the iconic clown (CLOWN) and the face of McDonald's hamburgers (HAMBURGER); one character cleanly reaches both.
items.pairNote: Solid character link in the BARNEY mould.

current.wordAConnection: Ronald McDonald is a clown
current.wordBConnection: Ronald McDonald sells hamburgers
current.revealExplanation: Ronald McDonald is the most famous clown ever to sell a hamburger.

items.reviewerReason: Grapes grow on vines (GRAPE) and tomatoes are sold as vine-ripened (TOMATO); the grape-tomato aside in the explanation is a nice bonus click.
items.pairNote: Watch board composition: other vine produce (melon, pumpkin, cucumber) on the same board could compete.

current.wordAConnection: Grapes grow on vines
current.wordBConnection: Tomatoes grow on vines
current.revealExplanation: Tomatoes and grapes both ripen on the vine, and there is even a grape tomato.

items.reviewerReason: Chopsticks originated in China (CHINA) and are the classic way to eat a bowl of rice (RICE); a clear shared scene.
items.pairNote: Explanation's 'rice is their perfect test' is slightly odd but not false.

current.wordAConnection: Chopsticks were first used in China
current.wordBConnection: Rice is eaten with chopsticks
current.revealExplanation: Chopsticks have been used in China for thousands of years, and rice is their perfect test.

items.reviewerReason: Popcorn is the movie-theater treat (MOVIE) and is itself a snack (SNACK); obvious but the natural best hint.
items.reviewerFix: Mention the snack side in the explanation, e.g. 'Popcorn is the snack that makes a movie night feel complete.'
items.pairNote: Easy pair; POPCORN is a hyponym of SNACK, not a synonym, so it is allowed.

current.wordAConnection: Popcorn at the movies
current.wordBConnection: Popcorn is the classic snack
current.revealExplanation: A movie just feels incomplete without a bucket of popcorn.

items.reviewerReason: Jalapenos are the everyday hot pepper (SPICY) and a standard taco topping (TACO).
items.pairNote: Fine; competes only if another Mexican food or hot item is on the board.

current.wordAConnection: Jalapenos make food spicy
current.wordBConnection: Jalapenos are a favorite taco topping
current.revealExplanation: A few jalapeno slices turn a mild taco into a spicy one.

items.reviewerReason: The Warriors are an NBA team (BASKETBALL) and Steph Curry's only team (CURRY), so it reaches basketball directly as well as through Curry.
items.pairNote: Both work; the explanation's claim about his whole career with Golden State is correct as far as I know but should be rechecked if he ever changes teams.

current.wordAConnection: The Warriors are a basketball team
current.wordBConnection: Curry plays for the Golden State Warriors
current.revealExplanation: Steph Curry has spent his whole NBA career with the Golden State Warriors.

items.reviewerReason: STEPH is Curry's first name (CURRY) and he is a basketball superstar (BASKETBALL), but the basketball side only comes via the person.
items.pairNote: Both work; the explanation's claim about his whole career with Golden State is correct as far as I know but should be rechecked if he ever changes teams.

current.wordAConnection: Steph Curry is a basketball superstar
current.wordBConnection: Steph Curry
current.revealExplanation: Steph Curry made the long-range three-pointer the heart of modern basketball.

items.reviewerReason: Toad is Mario's mushroom-headed sidekick (MARIO) and a mushroom character, with a 'toadstool' echo (MUSHROOM).
items.pairNote: 'Since 1985' is fair: the Mushroom Retainers (Toads) were in the original Super Mario Bros., though Toad as a named playable character came later.

current.wordAConnection: Toad is Mario's loyal friend
current.wordBConnection: Toad has a mushroom cap for a head (and a toadstool is a mushroom)
current.revealExplanation: Toad, the little mushroom guy, has been at Mario's side since 1985.

items.reviewerReason: Belgium is famous for waffles (Belgian waffle, BELGIUM) and waffles are a breakfast staple (BREAKFAST).
items.pairNote: Clean.

current.wordAConnection: Belgian waffles
current.wordBConnection: Waffles are a breakfast favorite
current.revealExplanation: Belgian waffles turn an ordinary breakfast into a treat.

items.reviewerReason: Two famous Charlies: Charlie Brown of Peanuts (BROWN) and Charlie of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory (CHOCOLATE); both are instantly familiar and the reveal is satisfying.
items.pairNote: Name-join across two works rather than one shared reference; I labelled it 'other'. It is name-based but exceptional enough to pass under the phrase-join guidance.

current.wordAConnection: Charlie Brown of Peanuts
current.wordBConnection: Charlie and the Chocolate Factory
current.revealExplanation: Good grief: Charlie Brown and the boy with the golden ticket share a name.

items.reviewerReason: S'mores are the campfire treat (CAMP) built around a chocolate square (CHOCOLATE).
items.pairNote: Apostrophe dropped for the one-word format; fine.

current.wordAConnection: S'mores are the classic campfire treat
current.wordBConnection: Chocolate goes inside every s'more
current.revealExplanation: No camping trip is complete without s'mores: marshmallow, graham cracker and chocolate.

items.reviewerReason: A comedy roast (COMEDY) versus a roast turkey (TURKEY); a true double meaning that clicks.
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: A comedy roast pokes fun at a guest of honor
current.wordBConnection: Roast turkey
current.revealExplanation: At a comedy roast the guest gets grilled; at Thanksgiving the turkey gets roasted.

items.reviewerReason: Croissants are a bakery staple (BAKERY) and are crescent-shaped, the word itself meaning crescent in French (CRESCENT).
items.pairNote: Explanation fact checks out.

current.wordAConnection: Croissants are bakery favorites
current.wordBConnection: Croissant is French for crescent
current.revealExplanation: Croissant literally means crescent in French, which explains the shape.

items.reviewerReason: Lava is molten (LAVA) and the cake side rests entirely on the dish name 'molten lava cake' (CAKE), so the hint is basically the missing word of one phrase that already contains both targets.
items.pairNote: Judgment call: some reviewers will pass this as the perfect natural hint. A less mechanical route for CAKE + LAVA is hard to find; VOLCANO (lava; volcano cake) is another option but is also a near phrase-join.

current.wordAConnection: Molten chocolate cake
current.wordBConnection: Lava is molten rock
current.revealExplanation: A molten lava cake oozes warm chocolate, much like a tiny volcano.

items.reviewerReason: Being hungry means having an appetite (APPETITE) and The Very Hungry Caterpillar is a beloved picture book (CATERPILLAR).
items.pairNote: HUNGRY is related to APPETITE but not a plain synonym (adjective vs noun), so no synonym flag.

current.wordAConnection: Having an appetite means you are hungry
current.wordBConnection: The Very Hungry Caterpillar
current.revealExplanation: The Very Hungry Caterpillar had quite the appetite before becoming a butterfly.

items.reviewerReason: Slides (SLIDE) and swings (SWING) are the two defining pieces of playground equipment.
items.pairNote: Flat but natural; a more playful option would rely on the dance or baseball senses of SWING and SLIDE (e.g. BASEBALL: slide into base, swing the bat), which might be worth trialling.

current.wordAConnection: Slides are playground staples
current.wordBConnection: Swings are playground staples
current.revealExplanation: Every playground worth visiting has a slide and a swing set.

items.reviewerReason: Down comforters (COMFORTER) are filled with duck down (DUCK), and 'duck down' as in crouching adds a bonus pun.
items.pairNote: The explanation could optionally nod to 'duck down!' for extra delight, but it is accurate as written.

current.wordAConnection: A down comforter
current.wordBConnection: Duck down is the soft under-feathers
current.revealExplanation: A down comforter is stuffed with the soft under-feathers of ducks or geese.

items.reviewerReason: Both candles (CANDLE) and crayons (CRAYON) are made mostly of wax.
items.pairNote: Clean.

current.wordAConnection: Candles are made of wax
current.wordBConnection: Crayons are made of colored wax
current.revealExplanation: Crayons and candles are both mostly wax, just shaped differently.

items.reviewerReason: A buck is simply slang for a dollar (BUCK, plain synonym) and 'dollar bill' is a mechanical compound (BILL), so the hint is a synonym of one target plus a fill-in.
items.pairNote: Needs a new hint that avoids the money sense of BUCK, or uses both money words indirectly, e.g. WASHINGTON (face on the one-dollar bill, the buck) or a route through the animal senses (bird's bill, male deer).

current.wordAConnection: A dollar bill
current.wordBConnection: A buck is slang for a dollar
current.revealExplanation: Ask for a buck and you will usually get a dollar bill.

items.reviewerReason: The saying 'April showers bring May flowers' links April directly to showers (SHOWER) and, through the saying, to flowers (FLOWER).
items.pairNote: Flower side technically belongs to May in the saying; some players may expect MAY, but April is also a spring-flower month so it holds.

current.wordAConnection: April showers bring May flowers
current.wordBConnection: April showers
current.revealExplanation: As the saying goes, April showers bring May flowers.

items.reviewerReason: A magnet has north and south poles (MAGNET) and the North Pole is the planet's top (NORTH); the magnetic and geographic senses of pole meet neatly.
items.pairNote: The explanation is a fair simplification: a compass's north-seeking pole points roughly toward the geographic North Pole (strictly toward Earth's north magnetic pole).

current.wordAConnection: Every magnet has a north and south pole
current.wordBConnection: The North Pole
current.revealExplanation: A compass needle is a magnet, so its north pole points toward the North Pole.

items.reviewerReason: Dwight Schrute is a star of The Office (OFFICE) and a Dunder Mifflin paper salesman (PAPER).
items.pairNote: Good TV reference; The Office is widely known to a U.S. audience.

current.wordAConnection: Dwight Schrute of The Office
current.wordBConnection: Dwight sells paper at Dunder Mifflin
current.revealExplanation: On The Office, Dwight Schrute is the most intense paper salesman in Scranton.

items.reviewerReason: Snakes famously shed (SHED) their skin (SKIN).
items.pairNote: 'Sometimes in one piece' understates it (healthy sheds are usually one piece) but is not false.

current.wordAConnection: Snakes shed as they grow
current.wordBConnection: A snake leaves its old skin behind
current.revealExplanation: A growing snake sheds its whole skin, sometimes in one piece.

items.reviewerReason: The Oscar is the top film award (FILM) and Oscar the Grouch lives in a trash can (GARBAGE).
items.pairNote: Excellent.

current.wordAConnection: The Oscar is the top film award
current.wordBConnection: Oscar the Grouch lives in a garbage can
current.revealExplanation: One Oscar sits on a movie star's shelf; the other lives in a garbage can on Sesame Street.

items.reviewerReason: Dora the Explorer's sidekicks are literally Backpack (BACKPACK) and Map (MAP).
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: Dora's talking Backpack
current.wordBConnection: Dora's talking Map
current.revealExplanation: Dora the Explorer never sets out without Backpack and Map.

items.reviewerReason: Darth Vader is the Star Wars villain (STAR WARS) famous for revealing he is Luke's father (FATHER).
items.pairNote: The film line is 'No, I am your father'; quoting the familiar fragment is acceptable.

current.wordAConnection: Vader turns out to be Luke's father
current.wordBConnection: Darth Vader is the Star Wars villain
current.revealExplanation: "I am your father" made Darth Vader the most famous dad in movie history.

items.reviewerReason: Mary Poppins floats in with her umbrella (UMBRELLA) and sings 'A Spoonful of Sugar' (SUGAR).
items.pairNote: Strong.

current.wordAConnection: A spoonful of sugar
current.wordBConnection: Mary Poppins floats in on her umbrella
current.revealExplanation: Mary Poppins arrives by umbrella and swears by a spoonful of sugar.

items.reviewerReason: Perry the Platypus (PLATYPUS) is secret Agent P (AGENT) in Phineas and Ferb.
items.pairNote: Kids' cartoon is widely known to younger adults and families; older players may need the explanation, hence moderate.
